\chapter{Afternoon}
\label{ch:ka-afternoon}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say \textquotedblleft{}afternoon\textquotedblright{} in Kannada and keep it distinct from noon.}

Say \kn{ಅಪರಾಹ್ನ}, split it into apara (\textquotedblleft{}latter\textquotedblright{}) + ahna (\textquotedblleft{}day\textquotedblright{}), and match that -ahna against the one in \kn{ಮಧ್ಯಾಹ್ನ}.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[\kn{ಅಪರಾಹ್ನ}]{\kn{ಅಪರಾಹ್ನ} (aparāhna) — the same \textquotedblleft{}-ahna\textquotedblright{} pattern, a different first piece}

\label{lesson:KA-C28-aparahna}



\begin{quote}
You already know \kn{ಮಧ್ಯಾಹ್ನ}, \textquotedblleft{}noon\textquotedblright{} — \textquotedblleft{}middle\textquotedblright{} plus \textquotedblleft{}day.\textquotedblright{} This lesson's word for \textquotedblleft{}afternoon\textquotedblright{} uses the exact same building pattern, just with a different first piece.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\kn{ಅಪರಾಹ್ನ}} (\textbf{aparāhna}) — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{afternoon}\textquotedblright{} — is a genuine \textbf{Sanskrit tatsama}: \textbf{\kn{ಅಪರ}} (\emph{apara}, \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{latter, further}\textquotedblright{}) + the same \textbf{-\kn{ಅಹ್ನ}} (\emph{-ahna}, \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{day}\textquotedblright{}) suffix already hiding inside \textbf{\kn{ಮಧ್ಯಾಹ್ನ}} (\emph{madhyāhna}, \textquotedblleft{}noon,\textquotedblright{} Chapter 17). Same clean two-piece structure, same \textquotedblleft{}day\textquotedblright{} ending — just swap \emph{madhya} (\textquotedblleft{}middle\textquotedblright{}) for \emph{apara} (\textquotedblleft{}latter, further along\textquotedblright{}) and you move from \textquotedblleft{}noon\textquotedblright{} to \textquotedblleft{}afternoon.\textquotedblright{} This distinction comes from a genuine, classical \textbf{five-part Sanskrit division of the day} — \emph{prāta} (early morning), \emph{saṅgava}, \emph{madhyāhna} (noon), \emph{aparāhna} (afternoon), \emph{sāyāhna} (evening) — with \emph{aparāhna} landing specifically as the fourth part, after noon and before evening.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{culture}
Here's where this lesson needs real care: some sources describe \textbf{\kn{ಮಧ್ಯಾಹ್ನ}} itself being stretched loosely in casual modern speech to cover the whole afternoon too — which would echo Hindi's own \dv{दोपहर}, attested to have genuinely widened from \textquotedblleft{}precisely noon\textquotedblright{} to \textquotedblleft{}the whole afternoon.\textquotedblright{} But the evidence for Kannada is \textbf{much thinner} than what backed the Hindi finding — general dictionary listings rather than clear, independently-confirmed usage sources. Treat this as a plausible, hedged parallel, not a settled fact the way \dv{दोपहर}'s widening was. \textbf{\kn{ಅಪರಾಹ್ನ}} remains the more precisely, formally correct word for \textquotedblleft{}afternoon\textquotedblright{} specifically.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}aparāhna\textquotedblright{} — \textquotedblleft{}afternoon,\textquotedblright{} apara + ahna
  \item the shared piece with madhyāhna — both end in \textquotedblleft{}-ahna,\textquotedblright{} \textquotedblleft{}day\textquotedblright{}
  \item the honest hedge — madhyāhna MAY also loosely cover \textquotedblleft{}afternoon\textquotedblright{} in casual speech, but this is far less certain than Hindi's dopahar-widening story
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What suffix does \kn{ಅಪರಾಹ್ನ} share with \kn{ಮಧ್ಯಾಹ್ನ}, and what does it mean? (\textbf{-\kn{ಅಹ್ನ}}, \emph{-ahna}, \textquotedblleft{}day.\textquotedblright{}) What's the difference in their first pieces? (\textbf{\kn{ಅಪರ}}, \emph{apara}, \textquotedblleft{}latter/further\textquotedblright{} vs. \textbf{\kn{ಮಧ್ಯ}}, \emph{madhya}, \textquotedblleft{}middle.\textquotedblright{}) Is the claim that \kn{ಮಧ್ಯಾಹ್ನ} also covers \textquotedblleft{}afternoon\textquotedblright{} in casual speech as well-supported as Hindi's \dv{दोपहर}-widening finding? (\textbf{No} — much more thinly sourced; treat it as a hedged possibility, not a settled fact.)
\end{tcolorbox}
